title: Trump takes aim at voting machines, mailed ballots and 2026 Midterms
description_short: Trump takes aim at voting machines, mailed ballots and 2026 Midterms
description_medium: On August 18, 2025, Trump used Truth Social to call for eliminating mail-in voting and electronic voting machines ahead of the 2026 midterms. He falsely claimed no other country uses mail voting and said he would sign an executive order about election administration. The post signaled a push to assert federal authority in a system largely administered by states.
description_long:
On August 18, 2025, Trump posted on Truth Social that mail-in voting and electronic voting machines should be eliminated before the 2026 midterms. He falsely claimed no other country uses mail voting, accused Democrats of cheating, and said he would sign an executive order to bring “HONESTY” to elections. Mail-in voting and electronic machines were both targets of the post, but it did not itself change voting rules.

The Constitution assigns much election administration to states, while Congress also holds authority over federal elections. A federal judge had already blocked Trump's earlier executive order, which sought to change voter-registration rules, election equipment and mail-ballot deadlines. The August post indicated another proposed intervention and pointed toward another court dispute over federal power.

Trump's statement renewed unfounded attacks on voting methods ahead of the midterms. It also moved the issue beyond rhetoric about fraud and toward another demand for executive control over election procedures.

title: Trump Signs $1.5 Trillion Tax Cut — Benefits Wealthy, Explodes Deficit

The enacted law lowered the corporate tax rate to 21 percent and changed individual taxation; its distributional and budgetary effects remain debated. The November 2017 CBO estimate concerned an earlier House version with a 20 percent rate and provisions that differed from the final law.

title: Trump Fires 17 Independent Inspectors General Overnight
description_short: Trump Fires 17 Independent Inspectors General Overnight
description_medium: Trump dismissed seventeen inspectors general in January 2025, removing independent watchdogs from multiple federal agencies. Lawmakers objected to the lack of required notice, and the dismissals removed experienced oversight officials. The firings raised questions about who would investigate agency misconduct and safeguard public spending, while their legality and the status of replacement appointments required separate consideration.
description_long: On the night of January 24–25, 2025, the Trump administration abruptly fired approximately 17 independent inspectors general at federal agencies, effective immediately. The mass purge — carried out via email without explanation — dismantled oversight infrastructure that Congress had built after Watergate specifically to detect waste, fraud, and abuse of executive power. Federal law requires the president to give Congress 30 days notice before removing an inspector general, a requirement the administration ignored entirely. Even senior Republican Senator Chuck Grassley, who had championed IG independence legislation, condemned the firings. Among those dismissed were IGs at the Pentagon, State Department, Transportation Department, and Department of Homeland Security. The abrupt sweeping removal of inspectors general — officers explicitly designed to be independent of presidential control — was described by government watchdog advocates as a deliberate dismantling of accountability infrastructure to allow the administration to operate without institutional checks.

title: Mass Deportation Campaign - 200,000 Expelled in 'Hardline' Operation
description_short: Mass Deportation Campaign - 200,000 Expelled in 'Hardline' Operation
description_medium: Trump expanded immigration enforcement through raids, removals and attempts to use wartime authority. The policies raised due-process and family-separation concerns as well as disputes over individual status determinations. Deportations, voluntary departures, detention totals and announced targets measure different parts of enforcement and should not be treated as interchangeable.
description_long: Donald Trump launched what experts characterized as a 'hardline,' 'maximalist' mass deportation campaign that expelled nearly 200,000 people through raids on sanctuary cities, schools, hospitals, and places of worship while using archaic wartime laws to bypass due process in the most sweeping immigration enforcement in U.S. history. ICE raids began January 23, 2025, with the administration reversing previous policies that protected sensitive locations, allowing immigration enforcement in schools and hospitals where families had previously felt safe. The campaign used the Alien Enemies Act - a 1798 wartime law - to quickly deport suspected immigrants with 'limited or no due process,' sending some to be imprisoned in El Salvador until federal judges halted the practice. Trump ordered the reopening of Guantanamo Bay detention camp to hold 'potentially tens of thousands' of immigrants, though logistical and legal difficulties prevented its use as planned. The administration's use of military planning through NORTHCOM and deployment of 15,000 troops to the border militarized immigration enforcement in unprecedented ways, with fears of ICE raids impacting agriculture, construction, and hospitality industries. Despite claiming 140,000 deportations by April, CNN reported ICE alone had deported nearly 200,000 by August, though the administration's numbers remained disputed. The systematic targeting included Colombian nationals, creating diplomatic tensions when foreign governments pushed back against deportation flights.

The pattern matched earlier warnings from voting-rights experts: draft power grabs can alter trust even when not formally signed.
description_long: Trump denied pursuing a draft executive order that would expand federal control over election administration. The proposal’s authorship, provisions and stage of consideration were not established.
notes: The public account does not establish who wrote the draft, what provisions it contained or whether it was formally presented to Trump.

title: F-35 Sales to Turkey Advance Over Israeli Objections
description_short: Administration advanced F-35 sales to Turkey in a transactional move bypassing geopolitical considerations. Sale proceeded despite strong Israeli objections.
description_medium: In July 2026, Trump said he was considering selling F-35 fighter jets to Turkey. Hours later, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told CNN he opposed the potential sale and questioned Turkey's reliability as a U.S. ally. Trump’s remarks and Netanyahu’s response showed that the sale was under consideration, not approved or completed.
description_long: In July 2026, Trump said he was considering selling F-35 fighter jets to Turkey. Hours later, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told CNN he opposed the potential sale, warning that Turkey was 'not exactly a model ally' and that selling it the United States' most advanced fighter would not make it friendly. Netanyahu also sought to downplay divisions between himself and Trump. The proposal remained under consideration, and Israel objected; no U.S. approval or completed sale was announced. The proposal did not establish that a formal transfer decision, congressional notification or contract had followed.
notes: No formal sale approval, congressional notification or contract is established.

title: Journalist Intimidation Infrastructure - FBI Director's 'Enemies List' Media Targeting
description_short: Journalist Intimidation Infrastructure - FBI Director's 'Enemies List' Media Targeting
description_medium: Kash Patel's published list of perceived adversaries and his rhetoric about pursuing government and media opponents raised concerns when he became FBI director. The list and rhetoric raised concerns that Patel would use federal power against perceived political opponents. A list and campaign rhetoric do not, without additional evidence, establish that every named journalist was investigated or prosecuted.
description_long: Donald Trump's FBI Director Kash Patel established systematic intimidation infrastructure targeting journalists, with civil rights organizations warning he 'presents a clear and present danger to the First Amendment's freedom of the press' through his history of filing frivolous defamation lawsuits and threats to prosecute media who reported on the 2020 election. Patel's appointment represented Trump's weaponization of the FBI against press freedom, with Patel having previously filed $119 million in defamation lawsuits against CNN ($50 million), The New York Times ($44 million), and Politico ($25 million) - all ultimately dismissed but not before forcing news organizations to spend years and resources in litigation. The systematic legal harassment strategy was designed to 'foment distrust of the media and promote narratives more favorable to President Trump' while creating financial burdens that could force smaller news organizations out of business or censor their reporting. Over 40 journalism organizations condemned the Trump administration's 'campaign underway in Washington to penalize independent reporting on the government,' noting the administration had banned the Associated Press from White House events and evicted longtime news organizations from Pentagon pressrooms while giving desks to pro-Trump outlets. Patel explicitly threatened media organizations, stating in interviews that the Trump administration would 'come after the people in the media who lied about American citizens who helped Joe Biden rig presidential elections,' demonstrating his willingness to use FBI authority to silence and punish journalists for accurate reporting. The systematic targeting represented what journalism organizations called authoritarian tactics to 'crush dissent, punish those who expose inconvenient facts and replace truth with propaganda.'
notes: The list and rhetoric alone do not establish that every named journalist was investigated or prosecuted.

title: Federal Agencies Place DEI Staff on Leave and Move to Dismantle DEI Offices
description_short: Federal Agencies Place DEI Staff on Leave and Move to Dismantle DEI Offices
description_medium: Following Trump's anti-DEI executive actions, federal agencies were directed to place DEI personnel on paid administrative leave and begin closing DEI offices. The action affected employees across government, but the stored claim that every federal DEI officer was fired overnight on January 20 is inaccurate.
description_long:
Federal agencies were directed to dismantle DEI programs following Trump's January 2025 executive actions. Implementation included placing relevant personnel on paid administrative leave and beginning to close DEI offices. The policy therefore affected both government programs and the employees associated with them.

Administrative leave is an employment action, but it is not the same as a completed dismissal. The immediate actions were administrative leave and office closures, not completed dismissals of every affected employee. The orders began a government-wide effort to close the offices and withdraw support for their work; they did not fire every DEI officer on January 20.

The administration sought to reorganize the federal government’s approach to diversity and equity. Its eventual personnel consequences would require additional evidence about specific agencies and later actions. Later staffing outcomes varied by agency and required separate personnel decisions. The closures continued over subsequent months.

title: Moodys Chief Economist Confirms Tariffs Have Done Significant Damage to US Economy
description_short: Moodys Chief Economist Confirms Tariffs Have Done Significant Damage to US Economy
description_medium: On May 6, 2026 Moodys Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi published a note stating the data are definitive that Trumps tariffs have done significant damage to the economy. A Congressional Democratic study released the same month found American households will pay an average of 2512 dollars in tariff costs in 2026, up 44 percent from 1745 in 2025, while consumers already face elevated costs from the U.S.-Iran war driving up energy prices.
description_long: Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi wrote on May 6, 2026 that the data showed significant economic damage from Trump's tariffs. Zandi presented an economist’s assessment, not a court ruling or a consensus forecast by all economists. A separate congressional Democratic study released that month estimated average household tariff costs of $2,512 in 2026, up 44% from $1,745 in 2025. The figures were estimates, not bills received by each household, and did not isolate tariffs from every other cause of higher costs. The two estimates did not show identical effects across income groups or establish a final annual outcome or a single cause for every price change.

title: Trump claims he will speak to Taiwan’s president, departing from decades-long diplomatic norms
description_short: Trump claims he will speak to Taiwan’s president, departing from decades-long diplomatic norms
description_medium: Trump claims he will speak to Taiwan’s president, departing from decades-long diplomatic norms. US and Taiwanese presidents have not spoken directly since Washington shifted diplomatic recognition to Beijing from Taipei in 1979 This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, legal development, documented relationship, or policy consequence linked directly or indirectly to Trump. The downstream effects include institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: On May 21, 2026, Trump said he would speak with Taiwan President Lai Ching-te. The proposed conversation would be unprecedented for a sitting U.S. president; U.S. and Taiwanese presidents had not spoken directly since Washington shifted recognition from Taipei to Beijing in 1979. Trump made the statement when reporters asked about Lai and referred to a “Taiwan problem.” Taiwan’s foreign ministry said Lai would welcome a conversation. No call had been scheduled, and the White House had not given a date or agenda. Direct communication could strain U.S.-China relations: Beijing views Taiwan as its territory and has objected to high-level U.S.-Taiwan contact. Trump’s statement signaled possible direct engagement but did not mean a call had occurred, alter U.S. recognition or settle Taiwan’s status. His language also sent mixed signals, offering contact while echoing Beijing’s framing of the Taiwan issue. No policy changed.
